excerpt: You do not need a plugin to add meta keywords in WordPress. Here are the safe ways to do it with a little code or the block editor.

faqs.a: Meta keywords are largely ignored by Google, but they can still feed some smaller search engines and internal site tools. If you want them, add them, but put your real effort into the title tag and meta description, which actually influence clicks.
faqs.q: Do meta keywords still matter for SEO?

faqs.a: Yes. The code-snippet method and the custom-field method in this guide work with any properly coded WordPress theme. Some block themes (full site editing themes) use a different header structure, in which case the dedicated SEO plugin route is simpler.
faqs.q: Will these methods work with any WordPress theme?

faqs.a: Paste it in the functions.php file of a child theme, not the parent theme. Parent theme files are overwritten when the theme updates, and you will lose your changes.
faqs.q: Where should I put the functions.php code?

faqs.a: The code in this guide uses a function that checks for duplicates and escapes the value before printing, so it is safe. That said, a typo in functions.php can break your site, so keep a backup or use the child theme editor carefully, and test on one page first.
faqs.q: Is it risky to edit theme files directly?

intro:
Meta keywords are the old-school meta tag where you list the main topics of a page, like 'plumber london, emergency plumbing, boiler repair'. Google stopped using them for rankings years ago, but some business owners still want them on their pages, either for smaller search engines, internal search tools, or simply for completeness.

The good news is you do not need a plugin for this. WordPress lets you add a meta keywords tag with a small piece of code or through the editor itself. This guide walks through three safe, plugin-free methods so you can pick the one that fits your comfort level.
keyword: how to add meta keywords in wordpress without plugin

body:
The meta keywords tag is a line of HTML in the head section of a page that lists words and phrases describing the page content. Years ago, search engines used it to understand what a page was about, and many site owners stuffed it with dozens of keywords.

That era is over. Google publicly confirmed it ignores meta keywords, and stuffing them does nothing for rankings. Still, a short, honest list of 5 to 10 genuinely relevant phrases harms nothing and keeps your page markup complete. If your reason for adding them is a specific tool, a client requirement, or a smaller search engine, go ahead. Just do not expect a traffic boost.
sections.heading: What the meta keywords tag actually does

body:
The cleanest way is a tiny snippet in your child theme's functions.php file. It adds a meta keywords tag to every page automatically, pulling the words from a custom field you set per post.

First, make sure you are using a child theme. Then open functions.php and add a function that hooks into wp_head, reads a custom field called 'meta_keywords', and prints the tag. The function should escape the value so nothing odd can slip into your page markup.

After adding the code, edit any post or page, open the custom fields panel, create a field named exactly meta_keywords, and type your comma-separated keywords as the value. Save, and the tag appears on that page. Pages without the field simply show nothing, which keeps your code clean.
sections.heading: Method 1: A small code snippet in functions.php

body:
If editing theme files makes you nervous, the custom-field-only route avoids functions.php entirely. Many themes print custom fields in the head if the field name matches what the theme expects, but most do not, so this method needs one small helper.

The practical no-code version is to add your keywords through the Custom HTML block placed in a widget area that your theme renders in the head. Honestly, that is unreliable across themes, which is why Method 1 is recommended for most people.

A middle path: use the free 'Insert Headers and Footers' style approach manually. WordPress itself has no built-in header-injection box, so without a plugin you are back to the functions.php snippet. The snippet is genuinely only a few lines, and once it is in place, adding keywords per page is pure point and click in the editor.
sections.heading: Method 2: Custom fields through the editor

body:
Block themes (the newer full site editing themes) work a bit differently because the header is built from template parts rather than a classic header.php file. The good news is that the wp_head hook still exists in block themes, so the functions.php snippet from Method 1 still works.

If you are using a block theme and want a fully code-free route, you can add a Custom HTML block inside the header template part and paste your meta tag there. Go to Appearance, then Editor, open the header template part, and add the block with your hand-written meta tag.

One warning: anything you paste into a shared template part appears on every page that uses it. That is fine for site-wide keywords, but if you want different keywords per page, use the custom-field snippet from Method 1 instead.
sections.heading: Method 3: For block themes and full site editing

body:
More is not better here. List 5 to 10 phrases that genuinely describe the page, separated by commas. Use the words your customers would actually type, such as 'emergency plumber camden' rather than single generic words like 'plumber'.

Do not copy your competitor's keyword list into your tag. It does nothing for you, and sloppy markup copied from elsewhere can introduce stray characters. Write your own list, keep it honest, and keep it short.

Avoid repeating the same word many times with slight variations. 'plumber, plumbers, plumbing, plumber london, london plumber' looks spammy and helps nobody. Pick the strongest few phrases and move on.
sections.heading: How to write a good keywords list

body:
After adding your keywords, check that the tag actually appears. Open the page in your browser, right-click, and choose View Page Source. Search for 'keywords' and confirm you see your meta tag inside the head section.

If the tag is missing, the usual causes are simple: the custom field name does not match exactly (it is case sensitive), the code went into the parent theme instead of the child theme, or a caching plugin is serving an old version of the page. Clear your cache and check again.

Remember the bigger picture. The meta keywords tag is a finishing touch, not a ranking lever. The elements that genuinely move the needle are your page title, your meta description, clear headings, and content that answers the visitor's question. Get those right first, and the keywords tag is just tidy housekeeping.

title: How to Add Meta Keywords in WordPress Without a Plugin
